title: AU Studio Rebrand
body: In the summer of 2025, following a rebrand from Studio Augie to AU Studio, we commissioned designer Sebastian Hunger-Bühler to develop new branding and a subsequent website redesign. Pulling inspiration from various sources, we landed on the concept of zoetropes with hand-drawn illustration. The brand assets consisted of logos, wordmarks, and animated gifs. We then got to work re-engineering the studio website, with a focus on displaying the wide range of styles and projects the studio executed upon. Following a series of intimate discussions, we landed on a splash page plus index format, allowing us to show work in both an overview and detailed perspective. Rather than present video in its heavy and unoptimized format, we chose to display the work through a series of gifs; breathing life into the site. What followed was an ever-evolving portfolio, gallery, and index. A site that allowed for growth without the pitfalls of confusion.

title: Blocks
body: Blocks was a series developed during my thesis. Drawing upon my previous Windows work, I set out to capture an entire city block. What followed was three distinct explorations. First, and to be honest most ‘low hanging fruit’, was the exploration of book form. I designed an accordion style book that allowed readers to unfold the city block, reinforcing its grandeur and the absurdity of its capture. Second, an interaction exploration. Taking advantage of my coding knowledge, I superimposed two versions of ‘my block’ into a single experience. This allowed viewers to further investigate the piece, inviting them to peer deeper by revealing windows through hover interactions. If desired, viewers could take a screen grab and create their very own window images, thus referencing back to my original works. Third, was a series of ‘Proposals of Space’. Leveraging an empty lot within my captured city block, I layered images from my personal photographic archive to explore possibilities within the ‘empty’ space. This became an exploration into the affordances granted to designers, while creating social commentary through selection of different landscapes and buildings.

Developing branding from a series of artworks allowed me to contribute across a number of mediums to various audiences.

title: Subject: D.B. Cooper
body: Subject: D.B. Cooper is a visual exploration and independent investigation into America’s most elusive skyjacker. While decades of research have failed to yield a definitive identity, the sheer volume of disclosed government files and media coverage has created a labyrinth of information. This publication pieces together articles and unredacted documents sourced from _The Black Vault_ online archive. Drawing inspiration from vintage newspapers and FBI dossiers, the design utilizes vibrant highlighting as a form of "anti-redaction"; a visual through-line that guides the reader through key discoveries and evidence. To contrast truth with speculation, articles later deemed fake or debunked are printed on stark black backgrounds, emphasizing the thin line between historical fact and true-crime fantasy.

title: Extractions
body: Extractions is a development of the Windows practice. Where Windows examined the city's architectural facades through a singular obsessive lens, Extractions turns inward; isolating objects from their environments entirely. By removing the background and flattening the subject, each image takes on the quality of a museum specimen or scientific illustration. The mundane rendered beautiful, the everyday made of potential.

title: F_RM
body: F_RM was developed as a direct result of my thesis. Beginning as a photographic research experiment, I drew inspiration from the window shape to inform a brand identity and institution proposal. I proposed an institution split into three pillars, form, farm, and firm. Form represents solo ventures; individual artists, projects, and works. Farm, collaborative efforts; group shows and lectures. And Firm, the institution as a whole. F_RM is conceived as gallery, school, foundation, and institution; a structure broad enough to hold the full breadth of creative practice. Exhibitions, panels, lectures, residencies. A space built to support the work, the conversation around the work, and the people making it.

title: Generative Furniture
body: Scraped Flickr using the platform's image API for media tagged with the single keyword "furniture"; collecting not just the photographs but the rich metadata attached to them: usernames, timestamps, camera models, geolocation strings, and descriptions written in a dozen languages. This project is an experiment in automated research, curation, and print-based layout. Everything from the layout engine to the covers was generated dynamically using JavaScript and Bindery.js, a browser-based book layout engine, utilizing little to no HTML. By letting the tool paginate and compose the material automatically, what began as a simple exercise in understanding a new program became a way to curate in tandem with the code itself. The result is a publication that exists somewhere between an intentional archive, a cultural catalog, and an attractive accident. An experiment in research and curation; exploring the vast array of Flickr images through the guidelines of a single keyword, "furniture". The images range from clear shots of chairs, sofas, tables to artistic interpretations of the word itself. At times, the odd image will sneak through. A motorcycle classified and tagged as a storage bench, a screenshot from what I can only suppose is a video game. From witty titles, like "Chairity", referring to a series of stacked chairs... to an image of an empty chair from 2015 titled "On Balkans, you can weight yourself on the street. Most often, this is the way to earn some extra money for people who retired and still want to stay useful".

title: Olivetti Book
body: This first issue in a series intended to explore the foundations and inner workings of heritage brands focuses on Olivetti, a renowned designer and manufacturer of typewriters and accounting machines. Olivetti was extremely successful throughout the 20th century and pioneered a variety of ideas, designs, and technologies. This collection of images and texts provides various points of view on the company whilst attempting to take the reader back in time. I dove into hundreds of archives, images, and essays to curate an overview of Olivetti and its lasting legacy on the design and typewriter landscape

title: Portfolios
body: ~~I've always remembered having a personal website. I remember, albeit vaguely, my brother leading me through the creation of my first site. The domain set-up, the tweaking of templates; the opening of a playground I'd explore for a long time to come.~~ Many of my portfolios and websites have come and gone, but my desire for experimentation and innovation has remained. While I can recall a number of my early websites, only a few remain. Beginning with my 'car door' portfolio, developed early in my learnings of coding, my fresh perspective on the space birthed experimentation. Now, many years later, my portfolio remains a continuously growing artifact. Years of rework and repositioning. Of time spent solving for various issues. A portfolio to a designer is like an outfit to a fashion baddie.

title: Studio Augie Website
body: I met Austin Augie in January 2024; he was living with the Amish at the time, in a small town in Indiana. He was looking to build a studio of his own, and a website to go with it. Very quickly, what started as a website grew into the building of a brand. Through a series of conversations and in-depth discussions, the studio began to take shape. Still called Studio Augie at the time, it would target three specific pillars — fashion, weddings, and events — and leverage Augie’s archive of projects and images. Over the course of a few months, I dug through hard drives identifying selects and organizing. By establishing those three pillars, we were able to exhibit a vast array of images and videos in an exhibitory manner. A challenging project, it paved the way for many learnings and the beginning of a blossoming business.

title: Sweat Shopping
body: I was commissioned to develop various marketing materials for a pop-up exhibition featuring three artists; Leah Tinari, Ori Carino and Robin Russell. I began by creating a double sided price sheet displaying the various pieces in the exhibition and their subsequent prices. These were handed out and picked up by viewers upon entering the space. I then created poster and flyer designs inspired by both the artists involved in the exhibition as well as the Lower East Side from which they gained inspiration.

title: Toyo Tsuchiya Website
body: Toyo Tsuchiya was a prominent artist in the Lower East Side of Manhattan in the 1980s during a period of Anti-Art (Neoism). Co-creator of NO SE NO Social Club and the Rivington School, Toyo’s archive spans thousands of silver gelatin prints documenting the artist scene of the 1980s — as not only a photographer, but as an individual contributor. Developed from this work was a structure to be built upon through the construction of his archive. The structure, contrary to a living artist’s portfolio, served to present the work as an overview, inviting curators and galleries to gaze upon the range of work. An inspiring force. I was honored to be a part of this work.

title: Victorian Short Stories Of
body: A curated publication of Victorian short stories exploring the dualities of romance and ruin. Two contrasting collections sourced from Project Gutenberg; _Victorian Short Stories of Successful Marriages_ and _Victorian Short Stories of Troubled Marriages_, bound into a single volume, the design physically manifesting the harmony and chaos of these relationships. The covers establish this tension through deliberate subversion. The front cover, introducing the successful marriages section, depicts the Crystal Palace actively engulfed in flames. The back cover, introducing troubled marriages, shows the building pristine and intact. Destructive passion on one side, deceptive calm on the other. Rather than a single unified table of contents, each section opens with its own; reinforcing the idea that these are two distinct books sharing a binding. The typographic system mirrors this split throughout: the successful marriages half is set in black ink on white, clean and traditional, a deliberately ideal reading experience at odds with its burning cover. The moment the content shifts, the book inverts entirely; white text on black, plunging the reader into a darker space. Period paintings were selected for each chapter opening, matched thematically to the emotional register of the story that follows.

title: Wikibook
body: "Thirty Five mm Film and Minolta’s SRT-101 in the Lower East Side” is an editorial publication designed by combining a series of Wikipedia articles with my photography. The result was a story, or description, of: film photography, my camera, and Manhattan’s Lower East Side. My TOC, made up by a combination of dots and breaks (loosely related to the amount of content in each section), is repeated on each chapter’s title page. The cover plays with the concept of hiding and revealing information, similar to what I was doing in my documentation of this particular neighborhood.

title: Windows
body: Windows is an ongoing photographic practice documenting the window forms of New York City's architectural facades. The window itself. Its shape, repetition, geometry. There is an absurdity to it: going out with a camera, flattening, curating, cataloguing. A body of work that became the foundation for a thesis, a brand, and several years of practice that followed.
